pairs.title: Sluice gate and flooded lane
pairs.version_a: Owen runs the night shift at a grain depot beside the Ash River. At nine p.m. the river rises fast. Owen opens the sluice gate on the east canal to ease pressure on the dam, as the manual says. The water runs down the canal into Harrow Lane, and eleven family homes flood, with ruined furniture and two weeks of repairs. Had Owen kept the gate shut, the water would have gone into the empty west field instead, which nobody uses. Nothing else in the system could have carried it there. Owen knew the canal led to Harrow Lane. He opened the gate to protect the dam, and the dam held.
pairs.version_b: Owen runs the night shift at a grain depot beside the Ash River. At nine p.m. the river rises fast. Owen opens the sluice gate on the east canal to ease pressure on the dam, as the manual says. The water runs down the canal into Harrow Lane, and eleven family homes flood, with ruined furniture and two weeks of repairs. Had Owen kept the gate shut, the water would still have broken through an old overflow ditch and reached Harrow Lane. Nothing else in the system could have stopped it. Owen knew the canal led to Harrow Lane. He opened the gate to protect the dam, and the dam held.
pairs.intended_difference: In version A the flood would have gone to an empty field had Owen kept the gate shut, so his action was the only route to the harm; in version B an old overflow ditch would have flooded Harrow Lane regardless of his action.
pairs.judgment_question: How much of the flooding of Harrow Lane was Owen's doing? Answer from 1 to 7.
pairs.comprehension_question: According to the account, what would have happened to Harrow Lane if Owen had kept the gate shut?
pairs.option_b: It would have flooded anyway, through an old overflow ditch.
pairs.option_c: It would have flooded only if the dam had broken.
pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers usually assign more of a harm to an agent when the harm would have been avoided by acting otherwise, but the ditch detail may lower the rating only partly, so I expect a moderate gap.
pairs.originality_note: A flood sluice with an alternative drainage route and a backup cracked ditch; it is not a trolley, bridge or chairman case.

pairs.title: Solvent room door
pairs.version_a: Tomas works the night shift at a print shop that stores solvent in a back room. The room has a rule, printed in bold on the outside of the door: keep it shut at all times. Tomas had read that sign on his first day and clearly remembered it. That night the room grew hot, so he propped the door open with a box to let air in. A ceiling fan had failed the week before, and nobody had fixed it. Around midnight a spark from an old lamp reached the open doorway, and the fumes caught fire. The fire burned the front counter and two walls before the crew arrived.
pairs.version_b: Tomas works the night shift at a print shop that stores solvent in a back room. The room has a rule, printed in bold on the outside of the door: keep it shut at all times. Tomas had come in through the side hatch and never seen that sign. That night the room grew hot, so he propped the door open with a box to let air in. A ceiling fan had failed the week before, and nobody had fixed it. Around midnight a spark from an old lamp reached the open doorway, and the fumes caught fire. The fire burned the front counter and two walls before the crew arrived.
pairs.intended_difference: In version A Tomas had read the rule and remembered it, while in version B he came in through another entrance and never saw the rule; the rule, his action, the fan, the spark and the fire are the same in both.
pairs.judgment_question: How much did Tomas's action cause the fire? Answer from 1 to 7.
pairs.comprehension_question: According to the account, had Tomas read the sign about keeping the door shut before that night?
pairs.option_b: No, he had never seen it.
pairs.prediction_rationale: Knowing a rule was broken tends to make readers credit the rule-breaker with more of the causal role, but the fan and the spark are vivid rival causes, so I expect a modest effect.
pairs.originality_note: A solvent storeroom with a rule sign on a door and two rival causes (a failed fan and a spark), with knowledge varied by which entrance the person used; not a chairman or dean case.

pairs.title: Roofer without harness
pairs.version_a: Hal is a roofer with fifteen years on the job. On a windy Tuesday he must fix a loose tile on a steep roof, and his safety harness is in the van. He decides to skip it, since the job takes only ten minutes. He knows the wind is strong and that a fall from that height could seriously injure him. He climbs up without the harness. A gust hits the roof. Hal catches the gutter, steadies himself, and climbs down with only a scraped palm.
pairs.version_b: Hal is a roofer with fifteen years on the job. On a windy Tuesday he must fix a loose tile on a steep roof, and his safety harness is in the van. He decides to skip it, since the job takes only ten minutes. He knows the wind is strong and that a fall from that height could seriously injure him. He climbs up without the harness. A gust hits the roof. Hal slips, falls to the driveway, breaks his wrist, and is taken to hospital.
pairs.intended_difference: The same decision to climb without a harness, made with the same knowledge and risk, ends harmlessly in version A when Hal catches the gutter and harmfully in version B when he falls and breaks his wrist.
pairs.judgment_question: How wrong was Hal's decision to climb up without the harness? Answer from 1 to 7.
pairs.comprehension_question: According to the account, what happened to Hal when the gust hit the roof?
pairs.option_a: He caught the gutter and climbed down with a scraped palm.
pairs.option_b: He fell to the driveway and broke his wrist.
pairs.option_c: The gust did not reach the part of the roof where he was working.
pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers tend to judge the same risky choice as more wrong when it ends in injury, though many will hold the choice itself fixed, so I expect a moderate gap.
pairs.originality_note: An everyday workplace choice to skip a safety harness, with a gust as the outcome-deciding luck; not a drunk-driver, surgeon or other standard moral luck case.
